title: Remove One Element to Make the Array Strictly Increasing
spaceBreakdown:
- int n, violations, i: scalars → O(1)
- input vector nums: modified in place, not counted
- no recursion, no containers allocated
approach: Scan left to right counting violations where `nums[i] <= nums[i-1]`. At the first violation, we must remove either `nums[i]` or `nums[i-1]`. If `i >= 2` and `nums[i] <= nums[i-2]`, removing `nums[i-1]` won't help (the gap remains), so we remove `nums[i]` by overwriting it with `nums[i-1]`. Otherwise we remove `nums[i-1]` (no overwrite needed, since `nums[i]` is the smaller value and easier for future elements to exceed). A second violation means one removal can't fix it.
hints: When you encounter a pair where `nums[i] <= nums[i-1]`, which of those two elements could you remove, and what condition involving `nums[i-2]` decides which removal is valid?

Greedy single pass. At the first violation at index `i`, remove `nums[i-1]` if `i < 2` or `nums[i] > nums[i-2]`; otherwise remove `nums[i]` by setting `nums[i] = nums[i-1]`. Example: `[1,2,10,5,7]` - at `i=3`, `5 <= 10` but `5 > 2`, so remove `10`.

**Already strictly increasing** - zero violations, answer is still true
`Input: nums = [1,2,3]` → `Expected: true`
⚠️ Bug: returning `violations == 1` instead of `violations <= 1` → returns false

**Two elements** - removing either leaves a single element, always valid
`Input: nums = [1,1]` → `Expected: true`
⚠️ Bug: requiring at least one violation to return true → returns false

**Violation at first pair** - `i = 1`, no `nums[i-2]` to check
`Input: nums = [5,1,2,3]` → `Expected: true`
⚠️ Bug: accessing `nums[i-2]` when `i = 1` without a bounds guard → undefined behavior

**Remove current vs previous** - when `nums[i] <= nums[i-2]`, must remove `nums[i]`, not `nums[i-1]`
`Input: nums = [2,3,1,2]` → `Expected: false`
⚠️ Bug: always removing `nums[i-1]` (skipping the `nums[i-2]` check) → returns true

**Two violations** - one removal cannot fix two separate drops
`Input: nums = [2,1,3,2]` → `Expected: false`
⚠️ Bug: returning true after the first violation without scanning the rest → returns true

followUps.q: What if you could remove at most k elements instead of exactly one?
followUps.a: Replace the `violations > 1` check with `violations > k` and apply the same greedy fix at each violation. Time O(n), space O(1).

followUps.q: What if the array length is up to 10^5?
followUps.a: The O(n) single-pass approach already handles this; only the O(n^2) brute-force "try removing each index" would be too slow. Time O(n), space O(1).

followUps.q: What if you must return the index to remove (or -1 if already increasing)?
followUps.a: Track a `removedIndex` variable: set it to `i-1` when removing `nums[i-1]`, or to `i` when overwriting `nums[i]`. Return `removedIndex` (or -1 if no violation occurred). Time O(n), space O(1).
